posts.title: How this site works: a static portfolio with a database behind it
posts.excerpt: Astro builds every page ahead of time, Supabase holds the content, and publishing a post rebuilds the site and shares it on LinkedIn — without exposing the database to the browser.
posts.body_md:
I wanted a personal site that behaves like a small LinkedIn I control: a profile, my experience, what I'm testing in my homelab, and posts I can share. I also wanted it to be boring to operate and hard to abuse.

## The shape of it

Every page is generated ahead of time by **Astro** and served as plain files from **GitHub Pages**, behind **Cloudflare**. There is no application server to patch and nothing to log into on the public site.

The content lives in **Supabase** (PostgreSQL). When I change something — a new post, a new lab, an updated role — a database trigger asks GitHub Actions to rebuild. A few minutes later the site is live again.

## Why the browser never talks to the database

The tempting design is to fetch content from Supabase in the browser. I did the opposite: the public key can't read anything. Content is read only at build time, with a key that lives in GitHub's secret store.

```sql
-- every content table: RLS on, no policies, no grants for client roles
alter table public.posts enable row level security;
revoke all on table public.posts from anon, authenticated;
```

That removes a whole class of problems: there's no public data API to scrape, and a mistake in a policy can't leak a draft.

## Sharing to LinkedIn

When a post is published, the deploy workflow waits for the new version to go live and then calls the LinkedIn Posts API with the title, a summary and a thumbnail generated from the post itself. Each share is claimed in the database first, so a post can never be shared twice.

## The contact form

It's the only place the site collects personal data, so it collects as little as possible: name, email, message, and the fact that you agreed to the privacy notice. Spam protection uses Cloudflare Turnstile, rate limits use a salted hash of the IP that's deleted after a day, and messages are deleted automatically after twelve months.

If you're building something similar and want to compare notes, the contact form works.

posts.title: From one to four Proxmox nodes: what my homelab is for
posts.excerpt: A business analyst with a server rack sounds like a hobby that got out of hand. Here's why it's part of how I work.
posts.body_md:
My homelab started as one Proxmox node. It's four now.

## Why a business analyst runs a homelab

When I recommend a tool, I like to have broken it first. Running ERP trials, workflow engines and AI models on my own hardware lets me answer the questions that matter to a business: how hard is this to operate, what happens when it fails, and what does it really cost?

## What's running

- **Compute:** Proxmox VE across four nodes.
- **Backups:** Proxmox Backup Server for the VMs, Kopia and rclone for offsite copies.
- **Edge:** Traefik v3 on an Oracle Cloud VM, with Cloudflare in front of anything public.
- **Network:** Technitium for internal DNS and DHCP.

## What I've learned so far

Backups aren't done until you've restored from them. The edge is where most of the interesting decisions are. And documenting a setup as you build it is the same discipline as writing good requirements: if you can't explain it, you don't understand it yet.

I'll share the individual experiments in the Labs section as they mature.
